cards.title: Phased array ultrasonics
cards.html: Phased array ultrasonics (PA) is an advanced method of ultrasonic testing that has applications in medical imaging and industrial nondestructive testing. Common applications are to noninvasively examine the heart or to find flaws in manufactured materials such as welds. Single-element (non-phased array) probes, known technically as monolithic probes, emit a beam in a fixed direction. To test or interrogate a large volume of material, a conventional probe must be physically scanned (moved or turned) to sweep the beam through the area of interest. In contrast, the beam from a phased array probe can be focused and swept electronically without moving the probe. The beam is controllable because a phased array probe is made up of multiple small elements, each of which can be pulsed individually at a computer-calculated timing. The term phased refers to the timing, and the term array refers to the multiple elements. Phased array ultrasonic testing is based on principles of wave physics, which also have applications in fields such as optics and electromagnetic antennae.

Single-element (non- phased array ) probes , known technically as monolithic probes, emit a beam in a fixed direction. To test or interrogate a large volume of material, a conventional probe must be physically scanned (moved or turned) to sweep the beam through the area of interest. In contrast, the beam from a phased array probe can be focused and swept electronically without moving the probe. The beam is controllable because a phased array probe is made up of multiple small elements, each of which can be pulsed individually at a computer-calculated timing. The term phased refers to the timing, and the term array refers to the multiple elements. Phased array ultrasonic testing is based on principles of wave physics , which also have applications in fields such as optics and electromagnetic antennae .

cards.q: In **phased array**, what does the word *phased* refer to?
options: The timing of each element's pulse
The phase of the mains supply to the set
The stages of a weld inspection
The way the crystal is cut
cards.why: The text says it plainly: *phased* is the timing, *array* is the many elements. Each small element is pulsed at a time the computer works out, and those timings shape and steer the beam. The mains supply and the crystal cut have nothing to do with the name.

cards.title: Principle of operation
cards.html: The PA probe consists of many small ultrasonic transducers, each of which can be pulsed independently. By varying the timing, for instance by making the pulse from each transducer progressively delayed going up the line, a pattern of constructive interference is set up that results in radiating a quasi-plane ultrasonic beam at a set angle depending on the progressive time delay. In other words, by changing the progressive time delay the beam can be steered electronically. It can be swept like a search-light through the tissue or object being examined, and the data from multiple beams are put together to make a visual image showing a slice through the object.

cards.q: Each element fires a little later than the one before it, going up the line. What does the beam do?
options: It leaves at an angle set by the delay
It stays straight down but gets stronger
It splits into one beam per element
It cancels out and nothing goes in
cards.why: The small waves from the elements add up (constructive interference) along a tilted front, so the beam leaves at an angle. Change the delay step and the angle changes: that is steering with no moving parts. It does not cancel: the delays are chosen so the waves line up in the direction wanted.
cards.hint: Think of a line of people stepping off one after another: the front they make is slanted.

cards.title: Use in industry
cards.html:
Phased array is widely used for nondestructive testing (NDT) in several industrial sectors, such as construction, pipelines, and power generation. This method is an advanced NDT method that is used to detect discontinuities i.e. cracks or flaws and thereby determine component quality. Due to the possibility to control parameters such as beam angle and focal distance, this method is very efficient regarding the defect detection and speed of testing. Apart from detecting flaws in components, phased array can also be used for wall thickness measurements in conjunction with corrosion testing. Phased array can be used for the following industrial purposes:

  • Inspection of welds
  • Thickness measurements
  • Corrosion inspection
  • PAUT Validation/Demonstration Blocks
  • Rolling stock inspection (wheels and axles)
  • PAUT & TOFD Standard Calibration Blocks

cards.title: Features
cards.html:
• The method most commonly used for medical ultrasonography.
  • Multiple probe elements produce a steerable and focused beam.
  • Focal spot size depends on probe active aperture (A), wavelength (λ) and focal length (F). Focusing is limited to the near field of the phased array probe.
    • Focal spot size = F λ / A
    • Near Field = A 2 / 4 λ
  • Produces an image that shows a slice through the object.
  • Compared to conventional, single-element ultrasonic testing systems, PA instruments and probes are more complex and expensive.
  • In industry, PA technicians require more experience and training than conventional UT technicians.

cards.q: Where can a phased-array probe focus its beam?
options: Only within the probe's near field
Anywhere, however deep
Only at the surface of the part
Only beyond the near field
cards.why: The text: focusing is limited to the near field of the array. Past the near field the beam spreads whatever delays you set, so deep focusing needs a bigger active aperture (more elements firing), which makes the near field longer.
cards.hint: The text names the region focusing is limited to.

cards.q: Against conventional single-element UT, what does the text say phased array costs you?
options: Dearer kit and more training
A slower inspection
Less control of the beam angle
No image of the part
cards.why: PA instruments and probes are more complex and expensive, and technicians need more experience and training. In return it is faster, steers and focuses electronically and gives an image of a slice through the part, so the other three are its gains, not its costs.

cards.title: Time-of-flight diffraction ultrasonics
cards.html:
Time-of-flight diffraction (TOFD) method of ultrasonic testing is a sensitive and accurate method for the nondestructive testing of welds for defects. TOFD originated from tip diffraction techniques which were first published by Silk and Liddington in 1975 which paved the way for TOFD. Later works on this technique are given in a number of sources which include Harumi et al. (1989), Avioli et al. (1991), and Bray and Stanley (1997).

Bray and Stanley (1997) summarized TOFD as tip-diffraction techniques which utilized the principle that the tips of a crack when struck by a wave will diffract the signals back to the other location on the surface. The depth of these tips can be determined from the diffracted energy.

TOFD was invented in the UK in the 1970s initially as a research tool. The use of TOFD enabled crack sizes to be measured more accurately, so that expensive components could be kept in operation as long as possible with minimal risk of failure.

cards.title: Principle of operation
cards.html:
Measuring the amplitude of reflected signal is a relatively unreliable method of sizing defects because the amplitude strongly depends on the orientation of the crack. Instead of amplitude, TOFD uses the time of flight of an ultrasonic pulse to determine the position and size of a reflector.

In a TOFD system, a pair of ultrasonic probes sits on opposite sides of a weld. One of the probes, the transmitter, emits an ultrasonic pulse that is picked up by the probe on the other side, the receiver. In undamaged pipes, the signals picked up by the receiver probe are from two waves: one that travels along the surface and one that reflects off the far wall. When a crack is present, there is a diffraction of the ultrasonic wave from the tip(s) of the crack. Using the measured time of flight of the pulse, the depth of a crack tips can be calculated automatically by simple trigonometry.

cards.q: Why does TOFD size cracks by **time**, not by how big the echo is?
options: Echo amplitude depends on how the crack is turned
Time is easier to show on the screen
Cracks give no echo at all
Amplitude cannot be measured in steel
cards.why: A crack tilted away from the beam gives a small echo even if it is large, so amplitude is an unreliable guide to size. The diffracted signals from the crack's tips arrive at times set by where the tips are, so time gives their depth whichever way the crack faces.

cards.q: A TOFD scan across a weld with a crack in it. Put the signals in the order they reach the receiver, first first.
items: The lateral wave, along the surface
The diffraction from the crack's upper tip
The diffraction from the crack's lower tip
cards.why: Each signal's time is its path length. The lateral wave takes the shortest path, straight along the top. A deeper point means a longer path down and back up, so the upper tip comes before the lower tip, and the back wall, deepest of all, comes last. The crack's height is the gap between the two tip signals, turned into depth.

cards.q: TOFD on steel (longitudinal, 5920 m/s). The probes' centres are {sep} mm apart and a crack tip lies midway between them. Its signal arrives {tt} µs after the pulse (wedge time taken off). How deep is the tip?
cards.work: Path $= 5.92 \times {tt} = {path:1}$ mm, so each slant is ${half:1}$ mm. Half the separation, $S = {s}$ mm. $d = \sqrt{ {half:1}^2 - {s}^2 } = {answer:1}$ mm
cards.why: The sound goes down a slant to the tip and up a slant to the receiver: two equal sides of right-angled triangles. Each slant is half the path; its flat side is half the probe separation; the depth is the third side, by Pythagoras: $d = \sqrt{(\tfrac{vt}{2})^2 - S^2}$. Halving the time as in pulse-echo, without the triangle, gives an answer too deep.
cards.hint: Distance = speed × time (5.92 mm every µs). Half the path is the slant from one probe to the tip; half the separation is the flat side. Pythagoras gives the depth.

cards.title: Applications
cards.html:
Phased Array + TOFD combination is commonly used to inspect pipeline welds.

Reliability

One of the limitations of TOFD is the "dead zone' created by the lateral wave signal just below the inspection surface (or OD surface in case of the pipe). The dead zone is approximately 5 mm and there is no flaw detection in this zone. Calibration blocks with side drilled holes as shown in Reference and ISO 10863 used to validate the "dead zone" and sizing accuracy.

Features

  • A computerised and automated system for weld inspection.
  • Probes are mounted on a buggy that travels along a weld, recording data as it moves.
  • Compared to conventional methods of ultrasonic testing, TOFD is sensitive to cracks and measures their dimensions accurately.
  • TOFD has a dead zone where it is not sensitive to defects, hence TOFD ought always to be supplemented by a conventional pulse-echo examination or phased array. The pulse echo probes are commonly mounted on the same buggy as the TOFD probes.
  • Requires ultrasound technicians with advanced training.

cards.q: TOFD has a dead zone of about 5 mm under the scanning surface. What should go with it so that zone is covered?
options: A pulse-echo or phased-array scan
A second TOFD pair, further apart
More gain on the TOFD receiver
A thicker layer of couplant
cards.why: The lateral wave hides anything just under the surface, so the text says TOFD ought always to be supplemented by conventional pulse-echo or phased array, often on the same buggy. More gain or a wider pair does not remove the lateral wave, and couplant has nothing to do with it.

cards.q: How does a phased-array probe steer its beam?
options: By firing its elements with small delays
By tilting the crystal with a motor
By changing the couplant
By using a different wedge each time
cards.why: The delay law sets when each element fires; the wavefronts add up in the chosen direction and focus at the chosen depth. A sector scan sweeps the angle electronically.

cards.q: What does TOFD use to size a crack's height?
options: Signals diffracted from the crack's tips
The amplitude of the reflected echo
The back-wall echo's loss
The crack's colour on the screen
cards.why: The tips of a crack scatter sound in all directions. Timing the top and bottom tip signals gives the height, and does not depend on how strongly the crack reflects.

cards.q: What is a main gain of phased array over a single-element angle probe on welds?
options: Many angles from one probe position
No couplant is needed
No calibration is needed
It works through air
cards.why: One probe can cover 40° to 70° in a single pass, with focusing, and record everything for review: faster and better documented than moving several fixed-angle probes.
